title: Radioactive decay
summary: Isotopes, mass defect and binding energy, alpha, beta and gamma decay, the strong and weak forces, half-life and background radiation, and (HL) the decay constant and activity equations.

keyterms.definition: Nuclides of the same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons.
Difference between the total mass of separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus.
Energy needed to separate a nucleus into its nucleons: E = Δmc².
Binding energy divided by nucleon number; a measure of stability, peaking near iron-56.
Emission of a helium-4 nucleus; A falls by 4 and Z by 2.
A neutron becomes a proton, emitting an electron and an electron antineutrino.
Emission of a high-energy photon from an excited nucleus; A and Z unchanged.
Time for half the nuclei in a sample to decay, or for the activity to halve.
Short-range attractive force between nucleons that holds the nucleus together.
Ionizing radiation always present from natural and artificial sources.
Probability of decay per unit time, λ; T½ = ln 2/λ.
Number of decays per second, A = λN, measured in becquerels.

questions.prompt: Which nuclide has the highest binding energy per nucleon?
questions.explanation: Iron-56 (and nickel nearby) is at the peak of the curve, so it is among the most stable nuclei.

questions.statement: The mass of a nucleus is less than the total mass of its separate protons and neutrons.
questions.explanation: The mass defect corresponds to the binding energy released when the nucleus formed.

questions.text: A mass defect of 0.030 u corresponds to a binding energy of about ___ MeV (1 u = 931.5 MeV c⁻²).

questions.prompt: Why do heavy stable nuclei have more neutrons than protons?
options: Extra neutrons add strong-force attraction without adding electrostatic repulsion
questions.explanation: As Z grows, proton repulsion grows; additional neutrons provide extra binding.

questions.prompt: Match each force to its role in the nucleus.

pairs.right: Holds nucleons together, very short range

questions.explanation: Nuclear stability is a balance of strong attraction against electrostatic repulsion.

questions.prompt: The strong nuclear force between two nucleons is
options: repulsive at very short separations (below about 0.5 fm), attractive at about 1 fm, negligible beyond a few fm
questions.explanation: Its short range explains why very large nuclei are less stable.

questions.text: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are ___ of each other.
questions.explanation: Same Z = 6, different neutron numbers (6 and 8).

questions.statement: Binding energy is energy stored in the nucleus that is released when it is broken apart.
questions.explanation: Binding energy must be SUPPLIED to separate the nucleons; it was released when the nucleus formed.

questions.prompt: Both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei release energy because
options: products have higher binding energy per nucleon
questions.explanation: Both move towards the iron peak, so the products are more tightly bound and mass is converted to energy.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to calculate binding energy per nucleon.
items: Add the masses of the separate protons and neutrons
Subtract the nuclear mass to get the mass defect
Convert to energy using 931.5 MeV per u
Divide by the nucleon number A
questions.explanation: Use nuclear (not atomic) masses or account for the electrons consistently.

questions.prompt: Radium-226 (Z = 88) undergoes alpha decay. The daughter nucleus is
questions.explanation: Alpha decay: A − 4 = 222, Z − 2 = 86 (radon).

questions.text: In beta-minus decay, the proton number of the nucleus increases by ___.
questions.explanation: A neutron changes into a proton, so Z increases by 1 and A is unchanged.

questions.statement: The continuous energy spectrum of beta particles was evidence for the existence of the neutrino.
questions.explanation: If only two particles shared the energy, beta electrons would have one fixed energy; a third particle (antineutrino) shares it.

questions.prompt: Match each emission to its property.

pairs.right: Fast electron, stopped by a few mm of aluminium
Least ionizing, reduced by thick lead

questions.explanation: Ionizing power and penetration are inversely related.

questions.prompt: A sample has activity 800 Bq. Its half-life is 2.0 h. What is the activity after 6.0 h?

questions.text: After 4 half-lives, the fraction of the original nuclei remaining is ___.

questions.statement: Radioactive decay is random: you cannot predict when a particular nucleus will decay.
questions.explanation: Only the probability of decay per unit time is fixed, so large samples follow predictable statistics.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a major natural source of background radiation?
questions.explanation: Radon from uranium in rocks and soil is a large contributor; phones and radios emit non-ionizing radiation.

questions.prompt: Gamma emission changes the nucleus by
options: turning a proton into a neutron
questions.explanation: Gamma photons carry away excess energy from an excited nucleus; A and Z are unchanged.

questions.prompt: Order the steps when measuring the half-life of a short-lived source.
items: Record the count rate at regular intervals
Subtract the background from each reading
Plot corrected count rate against time and read the halving time
questions.explanation: Background correction matters most when the source count rate becomes small.

questions.text: A nuclide has half-life 10 s. Its decay constant is ___ s⁻¹.

questions.prompt: A sample contains 2.0 × 10¹² nuclei with λ = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. Its activity is

questions.statement: A graph of ln(activity) against time for a single nuclide is a straight line of gradient −λ.
questions.explanation: A = A₀e^(−λt), so ln A = ln A₀ − λt.

questions.prompt: What fraction of nuclei remain after time t = 1/λ?
questions.explanation: N = N₀e^(−λt) = N₀e^(−1).

questions.text: The SI unit of activity, one decay per second, is the ___.
questions.explanation: Activity is measured in becquerels (Bq).

questions.prompt: A source’s activity falls from 640 Bq to 40 Bq in 20 days. Its half-life is
questions.explanation: 640/40 = 16 = 2⁴: four half-lives in 20 days, so T½ = 5 days.

questions.prompt: Match each equation to what it gives.
questions.explanation: Activity decays with the same exponential as the number of nuclei.

questions.prompt: To measure the half-life of a very long-lived isotope you should
options: measure its activity and the number of nuclei, then use λ = A/N
questions.explanation: For very long half-lives the activity barely changes; finding N from mass and molar mass gives λ = A/N.

questions.statement: Increasing the temperature of a radioactive sample shortens its half-life.
questions.explanation: Nuclear decay is unaffected by physical or chemical conditions such as temperature.

questions.prompt: After 3.0 half-lives, what percentage of the original nuclei have decayed?
questions.explanation: Remaining fraction = 1/8 = 12.5 %, so 87.5 % have decayed.
